MIA.summary:
- **De’Von Achane** — ESPN framed Miami’s offseason as a rebuild and noted the Dolphins have not extended Achane, who has one year left on his rookie deal at $5.767 million. The bigger takeaway is that Miami has moved on from major salaries while leaving one of its most fantasy-relevant runners unresolved. What happens next on his contract will matter for both roster stability and his 2026 workload outlook. [1]

- **Austin Clark** — Miami’s defensive line coach is now working with all linemen, not just the interior group. That broadens his role to include Zach Sieler, the 2025 rookie DTs, and edge players like Chop Robinson, Josh Uche and Ojabo. It suggests more unified teaching up front and gives the staff a cleaner way to align the run-game and pass-rush plans. [6]

- **Chop Robinson** — Clark said schematic changes and Robinson’s alignment should make things simpler for him, especially on early downs, as Miami tries to address his run-defense issues. Robinson’s playing time has been tied to that weakness, so improvement there would directly affect his snap share and overall upside. If the adjustment works, it could unlock more consistent edge usage. [7]

- **Benito Jones** — The veteran defensive tackle agreed to terms with the Raiders, ending his second stint in Miami after starting 23 games over the past two seasons. His departure comes as the Dolphins’ young DTs — Kenneth Grant, Jordan Phillips and Zeek Biggers — were already making enough progress to cut into his role late last season. That points to a youth movement in the middle of the line and less reliance on Jones’ veteran snaps. [8]

- **Bobby Slowik** — Jeff Hafley promoted Slowik to offensive coordinator while retaining him from the previous staff. The article says Slowik had been heavily involved across the operation in Philadelphia, and Miami is leaning on that experience as it tries to build a new offense and culture. What’s next is how much of that Eagles-influenced structure actually shows up in Miami’s 2026 offense. [3]

CAR.summary:
- **Rasheed Walker / Monroe Freeling** — Panthers GM Dan Morgan confirmed Walker and Freeling will compete for the starting left tackle job. Walker brings 43 career starts and a 93.8% pass block win rate in 2025, while Freeling is the high-upside rookie who fell to Carolina at No. 19. This is a real camp battle with both immediate protection and long-term lineup implications, especially with Ikem Ekwonu out. [4]

- **Bryce Young** — Dan Morgan’s latest comments appear to slow the momentum on a quick extension for Young, even though the Panthers have already picked up his fifth-year option. The team still sounds positive on Young’s future, but the timing of any deal is now less certain. That matters for Carolina’s cap planning and for how soon the franchise fully commits financially around its quarterback. [5]

- **Rico Dowdle** — The Panthers’ loss of Dowdle is framed as potentially costly after he led Carolina’s backfield in 2025 with 1,076 rushing yards and six touchdowns. Chuba Hubbard is back atop the depth chart, but the running back room also includes Jonathon Brooks, Trevor Etienne, and AJ Dillon. If the ground game stalls, Dowdle’s production will be a hard standard to replace. [7]

- **Panthers schedule** — Carolina’s 2026 slate is described as one of the league’s tougher ones, with a .521 opponent winning percentage and the 10th-hardest schedule. The Panthers will host Chicago, Denver, and Seattle and travel to Philadelphia and Pittsburgh. That raises the bar for early-season momentum and makes protecting Young and stabilizing the run game even more important. [8]

DEN.summary:
- **Taurean York (LB)** — The undrafted rookie linebacker is being viewed as a possible sleeper who could quietly push Broncos veterans for a roster spot. Denver signed York after not drafting a linebacker until Red Murdock, and York brings 39 SEC starts plus consecutive team-leading tackle seasons at Texas A&M. That matters because it adds real camp pressure to a linebacker room that has room for movement, with Drew Sanders specifically noted as injury-prone and underperforming. [4]

- **Justin Joly (TE)** — The fifth-round tight end said he’s ready to line up wherever Sean Payton asks, including the backfield or any spot on the field. Denver is betting on two rookie additions to raise a tight end group that underwhelmed in 2025. If Joly earns a role, it could matter in Denver’s two- and three-tight-end packages and in a room the Broncos believe needs more production. [6]

- **Jarrett Stidham / Sam Ehlinger** — Denver has kept Stidham despite reported trade interest earlier in the offseason, and the team’s QB depth behind Bo Nix is still in flux. The Broncos could consider moving Stidham if Nix is fully healthy, Ehlinger progresses, and Denver feels comfortable with Ehlinger as the backup. That would also open a roster spot and could force Denver to look for a third quarterback for the practice squad. [5]

- **Sean Payton / Broncos** — Denver is entering a tougher schedule context as a division champion, with the team already described as having a formidable slate against five last-season division winners and several playoff contenders. The Broncos are also being framed as vulnerable after an 11-game mark in one-score wins last year. That raises the stakes on how much the offseason additions and coaching continuity can hold up against a harder path. [8]

SF.summary:
- **Dre Greenlaw** — The 49ers’ post-draft linebacker picture has Greenlaw slotted in as the player they added to replace Dee Winters, with Fred Warner expected back from ankle surgery and fine for the season. The depth behind them is notable: Tatum Bethune has the most play-calling experience after Warner, Luke Gifford could keep the SAM role, and rookie Jaden Dugger is viewed as a special-teams first player with eventual SAM upside. That makes the room one of the deeper ones on the roster and leaves several backups fighting for niche roles. [1, 2]

- **Jaden Dugger** — The fifth-round pick is being framed as a roster-maker through special teams in Year 1, with possible future value as a SAM linebacker. If he can handle that downhill role, he could carve out snaps that few others behind the veterans can offer. [1]

- **Kurtis Rourke** — Rourke is competing with Adrian Martinez for the 49ers’ No. 3 quarterback job after spending his rookie year learning the offense. Offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak praised his arm talent, and the report says winning the third-string job would put Rourke on track to eventually back up Brock Purdy once Mac Jones is gone. [6]

- **Trent Williams / Colton McKivitz** — San Francisco’s tackle room is being viewed as a strength, with Williams still elite at left tackle and McKivitz described as a solid starting right tackle. Vederian Lowe is the swing tackle, Austen Pleasants made a start last year, and Enrique Cruz is a high-upside depth bet. That gives the 49ers much better contingency options than they’ve had in past seasons. [2, 7]

- **Ji’Ayir Brown** — Brown is drawing public criticism over his 2025 play, with Donte Whitner saying he was “no better than average” and calling out his deficiencies. The bigger fantasy/team takeaway is that Brown is still being treated as a questionable starter, and the depth behind him is also a concern. [2, 8]

BUF.summary:
- **Skyler Bell** — The Bills’ fourth-round wide receiver is being viewed as the first rookie with a real chance to start, with one analysis calling him the team’s first potential starter from the draft and projecting him as a likely WR3 by season’s end. That matters because Buffalo is clearly looking for help behind its top receiver options, and Bell’s quickest path to fantasy relevance is through a depth-chart climb. [6, 7]

- **Jude Bowry** — Buffalo used a fourth-round pick on the Boston College offensive lineman, and one assessment questioned the move because the Bills already had in-house options to replace their departing left guard and swing tackle. Bowry could still compete for a swing-tackle role, but the current roster math makes his path to snaps less clean than a typical fourth-round OL. [6, 8]

- **Jordan Hancock** — The 2025 fifth-round defensive back has gone from looking like a possible contributor to a cut candidate after Buffalo added multiple cornerbacks and safeties this offseason. Brandon Beane also said Hancock’s best position is not yet settled, so his roster spot may hinge on showing versatility during workouts and camp. [5]

- **Buffalo Bills defense** — Buffalo’s run defense drew another hard look, with one breakdown pointing out that the unit allowed 136.2 rushing yards per game and ranking 28th in the league. The concern is that the issue looks worse on deeper situational study, which suggests this is still a roster area worth monitoring even after the offseason additions. [3]

- **Offensive line** — The Bills’ line group is in transition after the departures of David Edwards and Ryan VanDemark, but the team has already added Austin Corbett and Lloyd Cushenberry and re-signed Alec Anderson. Chase Lundt is also on the roster, so Bowry is entering a crowded competition rather than an open door. [8]
